classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the area determines the sine of C rather than theta directly, interpret supplementary included angles as distinct triangles, and identify the unique maximum-area exception.

inlines.text: Is there enough information to find a unique value of
if the area of the triangle is given?

spec.description: Unshaded triangle ABC with a horizontal unlabelled base AB, A at lower left, B at lower right and C above. AC is labelled 15 cm, BC is labelled 10 cm and the interior angle at B is marked theta.
spec.mathematics: Two fixed sides meet at C. Theta is the angle at B, opposite AC. Construction coordinates preserve the source orientation and the 15:10 side ratio without adding printed measurements.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no angle values, calculated area or solution annotations.

answer.short: No, not in general. Supplementary values of $C$ can give the same area and two different values of $\theta$. At the maximum area of $75\text{ cm}^2$, however, $C=90^\circ$ and $\theta$ is unique.
answer.worked: The area rule gives $\mathcal A=\tfrac12(15)(10)\sin C=75\sin C$. Supplementary angles $C$ and $180^\circ-C$ have the same sine, so the given area can correspond to two triangles with different values of $\theta$. Therefore, $\theta$ is not uniquely determined in general. At the maximum area of $75\text{ cm}^2$, $\sin C=1$, so $C=90^\circ$ and the triangle has a unique value of $\theta$.
